processing: A clonal large-leaf cultivar, not a finished style. It is regarded as suited to black tea, made in the usual way by withering, rolling, oxidising and drying.
harvest_season: Not documented in detail for the cultivar; in Yunnan, spring picking is generally the most prized.
appearance_dry: As black tea, typical of Yunnan large-leaf: sizeable twisted strands, dark with golden tips in better lots.
appearance_liquor: As black tea, typical of Yunnan large-leaf: a clear, deep red-amber.
appearance_wet: Long-elliptic large leaves, coppery once made into black tea.
taste_profile: Noted for an orchid-like fragrance when made into black tea, over the fuller body typical of Yunnan large-leaf.

brewing.notes: General guidance for Yunnan black tea in a gaiwan; keep the first steeps short because large-leaf tea extracts fast.

vintage_note: Seldom sold under its cultivar name, so it is mostly anonymous within Yunnan teas. Made into black tea, it is normally sold as a recent harvest with the year stated. If a seller names the cultivar, ask for the season and the factory too.
description:
Yunkang 10 is a clonal tea cultivar from the Tea Research Institute of the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences, selected from the old bush population of Nannuo Mountain in Menghai. It is a tree-type, large-leaf plant with a national cultivar listing, and among the better-known modern Yunnan selections.

It is propagated from cuttings, so every plant is genetically the same, which sets it apart from the seed-grown population it came from. It is regarded as best suited to black tea.

The note singled out for it is an orchid fragrance. Beyond that, expect what is typical of a Yunnan large-leaf black: a full body and quick extraction, so short steeps in a gaiwan work well.

You are unlikely to find it on a label in most shops. It is grown widely across Xishuangbanna, Pu'er, Lincang and Baoshan, and has been taken to Sichuan and Guizhou, so a tea named for its region may well include it without saying so.
history:
The institute bred Yunkang 10 between 1973 and 1985, using single-plant selection from the Nannuo Mountain population in Menghai county. China's national crop variety committee recognised it in 1987 under the number GS13020-1987.

It was then planted widely in southern and western Yunnan and introduced to Sichuan and Guizhou. The breeding work won a second-class Yunnan provincial science and technology progress prize in 1996.
sources_note: Master list had green; moved to black because the only description says it suits black tea.
